hook.support: A message on a poster looks different from the same message in a video. Each one is made for different people. Learn to pick the right one.
hook.core: The same cause can show up as a poster at a bus stop, a webpage full of detail, and a 15-second reel. Same message, three very different texts. Each platform has its own layout, its own audience and its own rules. Pick the wrong one, and your message disappears.
hook.extend: Advocacy texts are shaped by their platform. A brochure, a webpage and a social post can carry one message. But their structures, features and audiences differ. Choosing the platform, and writing for it, matters as much as the message.

why.support: If you want people to hear you, you need to pick the right place to say it.
why.core: Whether you’re promoting a business, a club or a cause, you need to know which platform reaches your audience, and how to write for it.
why.extend: Media jobs, community groups and small businesses all need people who can adapt one message for many platforms.

articles.title: Same message, different place

body.support:
A **platform** is where a message appears. A poster, a webpage and a short video are all platforms.

You can put the same **message** on each one. But each needs a different **layout**.

**Poster**
- People look for about three seconds.
- Use one big picture.
- Use a few big words.
- Say what to do.
.
**Webpage**
- People come to find out more.
- Use headings.
- Give more detail.
- Add a button, like “Join now”.
.
**Short video (reel)**
- People scroll fast.
- Grab them in the first two seconds.
- Keep it short.
- Add words on screen. Many people watch with the sound off.
.
**Pick your platform.** Think about who you want to reach. Where do they look? Young people might see a reel. Parents might read a webpage.
body.core:
A **platform** is where a message appears: a poster, a brochure, a webpage, a social media post or a **reel**. Most **causes** and businesses use several. But one message needs to be **adapted** for each, because each platform has its own features and audience.

**Poster or flyer**
- Seen in passing, for a few seconds.
- One strong image, a short headline, a clear call to action.
- Logo and a web address or QR code for more.

**Brochure**
- Picked up and read for a minute or two.
- Folded panels, headings, short sections, photos, contact details.

**Webpage**
- Visited by people who want to know more.
- Headline and main image at the top, then headings, short sections, links and a big button (“Donate”, “Sign up”).

**Social media post or reel**
- Seen while scrolling; you have about two seconds.
- Hook first, then the message; captions on screen; hashtags; a call to action in the caption.
- Casual tone, but still clear.

**Choose for your audience.** Ask: who do I need to reach, where do they spend time, and how much time will they give me? A sports club wanting teen players might use a reel. The same club asking parents to volunteer might use a flyer and a webpage.
body.extend:
Organisations rarely rely on one text. A campaign’s core **message** is usually **adapted** across several **platforms**, each with distinct structures and features, and each reaching a different audience in a different context.

**Print: posters and flyers.** Viewed in passing. They rely on visual impact: a dominant image, a short headline, minimal text, a call to action, and a logo or QR code linking to more.

**Print: brochures.** Read briefly but deliberately. Panels, headings and short sections organise more information, with images, testimonials and contact details.

**Webpages.** Visited by people seeking information. A clear visual hierarchy (headline, hero image, headings, short sections), links for depth, and prominent buttons for action.

**Social media.** Encountered while scrolling. Content must hook within seconds, work without sound, and invite **engagement**: shares, comments, follows. The tone is often personal and informal.

**Choosing a platform** means matching audience, purpose and context: who must be reached, where they spend attention, and how long they will give. **Evaluating** an adapted campaign means asking whether each version suits its platform, and whether the message stayed consistent across all of them.

caseStudies.title: Slip, Slop, Slap goes everywhere

body.support:
In **1981**, a TV ad came out in Victoria. A cartoon seagull named **Sid** sang a short song. It went: **Slip** on a shirt. **Slop** on sunscreen. **Slap** on a hat.

The ad was made for the **Cancer Council**. Its message was simple: protect your skin from the sun.

The message spread. It went on posters. It went into schools. It became a program called **SunSmart**.

Later, two more words were added: **Seek** shade and **Slide** on sunglasses.

Today, the same message is on websites and social media too. It is the same idea, on many platforms.
body.core:
In **1981**, a cartoon seagull named **Sid** appeared on Victorian TV, singing a jingle: **Slip** on a shirt, **Slop** on sunscreen, **Slap** on a hat. The ad was made for Cancer Council Victoria. It became one of Australia’s best-known health messages.

The message was simple enough to work almost anywhere. It moved from TV onto posters, into schools and beaches. In **1988**, Cancer Council Victoria set up the **SunSmart** program to take it further.

In **2007**, according to Cancer Council Australia, the slogan grew to **Slip, Slop, Slap, Seek, Slide**: seek shade, and slide on sunglasses.

Today, SunSmart messages also appear online and on social media. The platforms have changed a lot since 1981. The core message is still easy to remember: five short words.
body.extend:
In **1981**, Cancer Council Victoria launched a TV ad starring **Sid the Seagull**, singing: **Slip** on a shirt, **Slop** on sunscreen, **Slap** on a hat. Three rhyming verbs made the message short, memorable and easy to repeat.

Its simplicity meant it could move across **platforms**: TV, radio, posters, school programs and beach signs. In **1988**, its success led to the **SunSmart** program.

Cancer Council Australia says the slogan was updated in **2007** to **Slip, Slop, Slap, Seek, Slide**, adding shade and sunglasses. Other sources date the change slightly differently.

Today, sun-safety campaigns also run online and on social media, platforms that didn’t exist in 1981. Each version uses its platform’s features, but the core message stays consistent.

The lesson for any campaign: a message that can be said in a few words can travel almost anywhere. The platform shapes the text. The message holds it together.

model.text:
**Cause:** our local Landcare group needs volunteers.
**Message:** Give two hours, plant 100 trees.
**Platform 1: poster at the supermarket**
- Photo: muddy hands holding a seedling.
- Headline: GIVE 2 HOURS. PLANT 100 TREES.
- Small text: Sunday 9 am, Lake Reserve. Scan to sign up.
**Platform 2: 15-second reel**
- 0–2 sec: a time-lapse of a bare hill turning green. Text: “This was us.”
- 3–12 sec: volunteers laughing, planting. Text: “2 hours. 100 trees.”
- 13–15 sec: “Sunday 9 am. Link in bio.”
**Why:** the poster reaches older shoppers in a few seconds. The reel reaches young people who scroll.
why: The message is the same in both: two hours, 100 trees.
Each version uses its platform’s features: a few big words on the poster, a hook in the first two seconds of the reel.
It explains which audience each platform reaches.

rubric.great: Short, memorable and the same in both.
Each is clearly made for its platform.
Judges which would work better, and why.

teacher.answers:
**Annotation:** 1 logo and navigation; 2 short headline carrying the message; 3 hero image showing the feeling; 4 headings and short sections for detail; 5 one big call-to-action button; 6 footer with contact details.

**Sort:** poster — bus stop; beach entrance. Webpage — how to apply, with links; season details for parents. Short video — 16-year-olds scrolling; how much sunscreen to use.

**Case study:** Slip on a shirt, Slop on sunscreen, Slap on a hat (1981, Sid the Seagull, for Cancer Council Victoria); TV, posters, schools, beaches, SunSmart (1988), now online; short and rhythmic, so it travels; Seek and Slide added (Cancer Council Australia says 2007).

realityCheck: **The date of “Seek, Slide” varies by source (2005–2010).** The course uses Cancer Council Australia’s date and says so at extend level.
**Students may want to make real posts.** Keep them in the workbook or a private mock-up unless your school has a consent process.
**Sid the Seagull is retro.** That’s the point: compare how platforms have changed while the message hasn’t.
**Works in a real class:** yes. The landcare-style model gives a clear pattern to copy.

levels.core: Aimed at about Years 5–6 reading: the standard version with four platforms, platform choice and reasons.
levels.extend: Aimed at about Year 7 and up: visual hierarchy, engagement, consistency across platforms, and evaluation.
